item.title: EleutherAI releases GPT-NeoX 2.0 for large-scale language model training
item.description:
EleutherAI releases GPT-NeoX 2.0 for large-scale language model training

EleutherAI has announced version 2.0 of the GPT‑NeoX library, a framework for training massive autoregressive language models on GPU clusters. The update moves the codebase onto the latest DeepSpeed release and adds versioned releases for backward compatibility.

🔍 Overview

  • Implementation of model‑parallel autoregressive transformers on GPUs.
  • Built on NVIDIA’s Megatron Language Model and augmented with DeepSpeed techniques and novel optimizations.
  • Repository records EleutherAI’s library for training large‑scale language models on GPUs.

🧩 How it works

  • Employs model parallelism to distribute transformer layers across multiple GPUs.
  • Supports launch via Slurm, MPI, and the IBM Job Step Manager.
  • Executed at scale on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs on platforms such as AWS, CoreWeave, ORNL Summit, ORNL Frontier, LUMI, and CINECA Leonardo.

⚙️ Key details

  • Two versioned releases are provided:
    • Version 2.0 – built on the latest upstream DeepSpeed and maintained going forward.
    • Version 1.0 – snapshots of the older stack used for GPT‑NeoX‑20B and the Pythia Suite.
  • Prior to 3/9/2023, GPT‑NeoX relied on DeeperSpeed, which was based on DeepSpeed 0.3.15.
  • Leverages many of the same features as the Megatron‑DeepSpeed library but with increased usability and novel optimizations.
  • Not intended for generic inference; for inference‑only needs, Hugging Face transformers is recommended.

🚀 Availability & Adoption

  • More than 40 organizations in academia, industry, and government have used GPT‑NeoX to train over 50 models.
  • Notable model families include:
    • Pythia (EleutherAI)
    • StableLM (Stability AI)
    • RedPajama‑INCITE (Together.ai)
    • FORGE (Oak Ridge National Lab)
    • Sarashina1 (SB Intuitions)
    • TildeOpen‑30B (Tilde)
  • Evo 2 from the Arc Institute was trained with Savanna, a framework derived from GPT‑NeoX.
  • A full list of models and publications is maintained in USERS.md.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a centralized, accessible location for techniques that train large‑scale autoregressive language models.
  • Accelerates research into large‑scale training by offering a usable, versioned codebase and support for diverse HPC environments.

#GPTNeoX #EleutherAI #DeepSpeed #LargeScaleTraining

Source: EleutherAI/gpt-neox

item.title: NVIDIA Introduces Daviator and Mixed Precision for DFT GPU Acceleration
item.description:
NVIDIA Introduces Daviator and Mixed Precision for DFT GPU Acceleration

NVIDIA has introduced two new capabilities to address performance bottlenecks in generating ground-truth data for machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs): a library called Daviator for batched GPU kernels and a new mixed-precision execution layer. These updates target the high volume of density functional theory (DFT) calculations required to train next-generation models, offering up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution.

🔍 The Problem with Current GPU DFT

Training MLIPs requires tens to hundreds of millions of DFT calculations. Plane-wave DFT, primarily implemented via VASP, is the standard for this task. While VASP’s OpenACC implementation speeds up large-system calculations, it struggles with the small unit cells and dense k-point grids common in MLIP data generation.

In periodic systems with small unit cells, hundreds to thousands of k-points are required. Currently, VASP processes these k-points sequentially on the GPU. For small systems, this results in significant kernel launch overhead that dominates compute time. A single-atom iron system with 752 k-points, for instance, ran 8x slower on GPU hardware than on CPU. Additionally, modern NVIDIA GPUs are increasingly optimized for lower-precision data types (FP32), while traditional DFT runs in FP64, creating a gap in available throughput.

🧩 How Daviator and Mixed Precision Work

Daviator is a library of GPU kernels that replaces sequential per-k-point processing with batched operations. Its core is a batched Davidson eigensolver that swaps sequential loops for batched FFTs, GEMMs, and custom kernels. This approach reduces GPU kernel launches, allowing Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) occupancy to reach near saturation. Data remains resident in GPU memory, while VASP retains ownership of the self-consistent field (SCF) loop, mixing, symmetry, and I/O.

The mixed-precision execution layer enables further performance gains by leveraging GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 throughput ratio. This is particularly effective on inference-class and workstation GPUs, such as the RTX PRO 6000, which features a 64:1 FP32:FP64 ratio.

⚙️ Key Details and Benchmarks

  • Integration: Daviator is accessible through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice by setting LDAVIATOR=True in the INCAR file. Existing VASP inputs work without modification.
  • Performance: On a projected reference dataset workload, the combination of these features shows up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution.
  • Speed-ups: Daviator overcomes OpenACC limitations, achieving over 2x speed-ups relative to the CPU baseline for a single iron atom.
  • Configuration: Users must set specific environment variables to ensure efficient kernel caching:
    • export CUDA_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/cudacache
    • export CUDA_CACHE_DISABLE=0

🚀 Availability and Limitations

Daviator is currently available for single-node execution. Multi-node support, coverage for systems with non-collinear spins (vasp_ncl), and explicit gamma-only runs (vasp_gam) are expected in a later stage. Some GPU kernels may trigger compilation on first use depending on the batch size.

💡 Why It Matters

As AI workloads drive GPU hardware development toward lower-precision data types, the stagnation of FP64-only code performance threatens the scalability of DFT data generation. By addressing small-system GPU inefficiency and leveraging mixed precision, these capabilities allow researchers to generate the massive datasets required for MLIP training more efficiently and at a lower cost.

#DFT #VASP #GPUComputing #HPC #MLIP #NVIDIA

Source: Tackling GPU Bottlenecks in Plane-Wave DFT with K-Point Batching and Mixed Precision | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Slurm 26.11 Introduces HRES to Enable Native Quantum Processor Scheduling
item.description:
Slurm 26.11 Introduces HRES to Enable Native Quantum Processor Scheduling

Slurm 26.11 adds Hierarchical Resources (HRES) plugins that enable quantum processing units (QPUs) to be scheduled as native cluster resources, allowing HPC centers to integrate quantum accelerators alongside traditional supercomputing systems.

🔍 Overview

National programs across North America, Europe, and Asia are integrating quantum processing units (QPUs) into supercomputing centers worldwide. These QPUs operate as cluster-wide accelerators, distinct from node-attached GPUs.

🧩 How it works

The HRES plugin interface uses short, portable Lua scripts to manage QPU scheduling:

  • Reports device health to the scheduler
  • Accepts device options as part of resource requests
  • Runs setup and teardown code at each job stage
  • Describes QPUs to HPC software via QRMI and QDMI open source efforts

⚙️ Key details

The architecture differs fundamentally from GPU scheduling:

Feature GRES (GPUs) HRES (QPUs)
Scope Per compute node Cluster-wide
Management Built into Slurm Plugin-based
Access Jobs on specific node Jobs on allowed nodes

A QPU is modeled using a single layer in resources.yaml covering nodes that can reach the device, with a count of one. The plugin logic is separate from site configuration, allowing vendors to distribute it across installations.

🚀 Availability

HRES entered Slurm in version 25.05 as a beta feature and reached production maturity in version 26.11, representing an evolution of the licensing mechanism with similar counting semantics but node-specific associations.

#Slurm #QuantumComputing #HPC #Supercomputing #QPU #Scheduling

Source: Integrating QPUs into Supercomputing Centers Using Slurm HRES Plugins | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: cuBLAS Enhances FP64 Performance Using Integer Tensor Cores
item.description:
cuBLAS Enhances FP64 Performance Using Integer Tensor Cores

NVIDIA cuBLAS now provides automatic acceleration for DGEMM (real 64-bit floating-point) and ZGEMM (complex 64-bit floating-point) operations without requiring application code changes. This capability leverages the Automatic Dynamic Precision (ADP) framework to map FP64 arithmetic onto integer Tensor Cores while maintaining native FP64 accuracy.

🧩 How it works

cuBLAS breaks double-precision numbers into integer pieces, performs multiplication on the GPU’s Tensor Cores, and reassembles the results. Both the Ozaki and 2M schemes align input matrix exponents and convert them to a shared-exponent, variable-length integer representation for accurate accumulation.

Algorithm Function Efficiency Detail
Ozaki-I DGEMM Grows with the square of the slice count
Ozaki-II DGEMM Uses Chinese Remainder Theorem; linear scaling in number of moduli
2M ZGEMM Cuts complex matrix multiplication from four real multiplications to two

⚙️ Key details

  • Heuristics: cuBLAS automatically selects between Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II for optimal performance.
  • Memory Management: cuBLAS utilizes memory-parsimonious tiling, discarding residue pairs immediately after their corresponding GEMM operation.
  • Fallback: The system reverts to native FP64 MMA instructions if the required mantissa bits exceed library defaults or user-defined limits.
  • New Format: Rubin GPUs utilize the TI16 format (12-bit integer) to accelerate Ozaki computations via the tcgen05.mma instruction.

🚀 Performance Metrics

  • DGEMM (Ozaki-II): Achieves 5.5x and 3.9x speedups on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and GB200 respectively. Throughput reaches up to 175, 147, and 37 TFLOPS on VR NVL72, GB200, and RTX PRO 6000.
  • ZGEMM (2M): Achieves a 5x speedup over native Complex FP64 on the NVIDIA GB200.
  • End-to-End (CCSD): Achieves 2x and 1.4x speedups on VR NVL72 and GB200 using DGEMM with Ozaki-II.
  • End-to-End (BerkeleyGW): Achieves 6.6x and 3.9x speedups using ZGEMM with the 2M algorithm.

#NVIDIA #cuBLAS #GPU #HPC #TensorCores

Source: Faster Scientific Simulations with New FP64 Algorithms in NVIDIA cuBLAS | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam Accelerates Black Hole Interferometry Processing
item.description:
NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam Accelerates Black Hole Interferometry Processing

NVIDIA has introduced cuPhoton.xBeam, a GPU-based FX correlator within the cuPhoton toolkit designed to accelerate the processing of radio astronomical data used to image black holes. Developed in collaboration with the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and the MIT Haystack Observatory, this technology addresses the significant computational demands of very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI).

🔍 Overview

Imaging distant, small-scale black holes like M87* requires capturing radio emissions from gas outside the event horizon using globally distributed telescope stations. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) links these stations to record high-speed voltage streams, producing petabytes of data that must be synchronized and correlated to reconstruct images.

🧩 How it works

Interferometry involves correlating signals from pairs of telescopes to produce complex visibilities, which sample Fourier components of the sky’s brightness. The cuPhoton.xBeam component organizes these radio signals for parallel processing on GPUs:

Feature Function
Data Indexing Indexes VDIF frames by timestamp, thread, and physical location via .vdix sidecars
Correlation Correlates signals between telescope pairs to produce complex visibilities
Data Tracking Explicitly tracks missing or invalid data without rewriting recordings

⚙️ Key details

Performance testing demonstrated significant improvements in data processing speed:

  • Execution: Processed a 10 TB dataset in 70 seconds on an NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 system with 64 GPUs.
  • Efficiency: Achieved a 460x speedup compared to an x86 CPU baseline of 31,992 seconds.
  • Infrastructure: Utilizes GPUDirect Storage (GDS) in compatibility mode for high-speed data ingestion.

💡 Why it matters

Future initiatives, such as the next-generation EHT (ngEHT) and the proposed Black Hole Explorer (BHEX), aim to improve image quality and measure the photon ring near a black hole’s shadow. The current cuPhoton.xBeam tool provides a scalable pipeline to handle the massive data rates generated by these observation arrays, enabling researchers to construct 3D gas models from visibility data.

#Astronomy #GPUComputing #Interferometry #NVIDIA #DataProcessing

Source: Run GPU-Powered Black Hole Interferometry with NVIDIA cuPhoton | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Correlated Expert Placement and Token Shuffling Cut MoE Training Overhead
item.description:
Correlated Expert Placement and Token Shuffling Cut MoE Training Overhead

Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) layers replace the feed‑forward block of a Transformer with E expert networks, routing each token to k experts. When experts are spread across GPUs under expert parallelism (EP), every MoE layer must perform all‑to‑all collectives in both forward and backward passes to dispatch tokens and then combine results.

🔍 Overview

  • On a cluster of 8 AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs per node, all‑to‑all communication can dominate training: 45 % of a step at EP32 with top‑2 routing and 60 % with top‑6 routing.
  • Early in pre‑training, routers already learn correlated expert selection: at top‑2, only 0.8 % of expert pairs in a layer are chosen together, yet they account for 42 % of token assignments, and the experts a token picks in one layer predict its picks in the next layer.

🧩 How MoE Works

  • Expert parallelism (EP) distributes experts across GPUs.
  • Each token is routed to k experts (top‑2 or top‑6 routing are common).
  • All‑to‑all collectives move tokens to the GPUs that host the selected experts, then gather the computed results.

⚙️ Communication Bottleneck

  • The all‑to‑all step is expensive because tokens frequently travel between GPUs and even across nodes.
  • At EP32, the collective alone consumes up to 60 % of the training step (top‑6 routing).

🚀 Optimizations

1️⃣ Correlated Expert Placement

  • Experts that are often selected together are placed on the same GPU.
  • A dispatcher that sends each token to each GPU once removes up to 58 % of dispatched rows.

2️⃣ Token Shuffling

  • When sequence parallelism shards tokens across the EP group, each token is moved during the reduce‑scatter that follows attention to the GPU predicted to hold its next‑layer experts.
  • On a single node this raises the share of token‑expert assignments served locally from 12.5 % to 59 %.

📈 Results

  • Across EP degrees 8‑64 in Megatron‑LM, the two methods together:
    • Reduce all‑to‑all time by 1.16‑2.63×.
    • Reduce end‑to‑end step time by up to 1.41×.
  • Neither optimization alters the model’s routing decisions or expert parameters.

💡 Why It Matters

By exploiting the natural correlated patterns learned by MoE routers, these techniques dramatically cut communication overhead without changing model behavior, enabling faster and more scalable training of large MoE models.

#MoE #GPU #Parallelism #DeepLearning #TrainingEfficiency

Source: Expert Coupling in MoE Pretraining: Reducing All-to-All Overhead with Correlated Placement and Token Shuffling

item.title: NVIDIA cuPhoton GPU Toolkit Accelerates End-to-End Astronomical Image Processing
item.description:
NVIDIA cuPhoton GPU Toolkit Accelerates End-to-End Astronomical Image Processing

NVIDIA released cuPhoton 0.1.3, an open‑source CUDA‑X toolkit that moves the entire image‑processing path for astronomy, laser, and X‑ray data onto the GPU, collapsing wait times from seconds to minutes and enabling interactive analysis.

🔍 Overview

  • Modern observatories and high‑throughput instruments generate image data faster than CPU‑bound pipelines can process it.
  • The bottleneck spans the whole path: sensor readout, point‑spread‑function (PSF) matching, subtraction, fitting, classification, and alert generation.
  • A GPU‑native path that stays on the GPU from sensor to decision is missing – cuPhoton provides exactly that.

🧩 How it Works

  • cuPhoton implements each stage of the pipeline as GPU‑accelerated building blocks, keeping data resident on the GPU.
  • Typical workflow steps include:
    1. xDataReader – Loads raw sensor data directly into GPU memory.
    2. xRep – Handles PSF‑matching and image subtraction.
    3. xPois – Performs statistical processing of photon events.
    4. xFit – Fits dual‑PSF models to dipoles produced by moving objects.
    5. xScan – Classifies detections as transients or artifacts.
    6. xRay – Specialized for time‑domain X‑ray detector analysis.
Component Role
xDataReader GPU‑resident image loading
xRep PSF‑match and subtraction
xPois Photon‑event processing
xFit Dual‑PSF fitting
xScan Classification of detections
xRay X‑ray time‑domain analysis

⚙️ Key Details

  • Performance: On workloads of hundreds of terabytes, cuPhoton achieved up to 14,900× speedup for image loading and up to 14,550× for signal processing, turning months of CPU time into minutes.
  • End‑to‑end impact: Data analytics that previously required nine months completed in four hours on GPU‑accelerated Python.
  • Latency: For kilobyte‑scale datasets, the entire pipeline runs in milliseconds or microseconds.
  • Scaling: Works on multi‑GPU, multi‑node systems such as NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and NVIDIA Vera Rubin.
  • Supported environments: cuPhoton 0.1.3 runs on Linux with Python 3.12–3.14 and CUDA 13. Building from source needs a C++17 compiler, CUDA and cuFile headers, and a re‑entrant CFITSIO installation.

🚀 Availability 

1

git clone --branch v0.1.3 --depth 1 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuPhoton.git

The toolkit is open‑source and part of the NVIDIA CUDA‑X ecosystem.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Instruments like the NSF‑DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory capture a 3.2‑gigapixel exposure every 39 seconds, producing up to 20 TB of images and 10 million candidate objects per night.
  • The Prompt Processing pipeline must classify ~10,000 detections within 60–120 seconds; cuPhoton’s GPU‑resident path makes such rapid turnaround feasible.
  • By eliminating the CPU‑bound bottleneck, researchers can iterate interactively, extract insights faster, and keep pace with ever‑growing data volumes.

#GPUComputing #Astronomy #NVIDIA

Source: Faster Scientific Image Analysis with NVIDIA cuPhoton | NVIDIA Technical Blog
